THE ETHICS OF GREECE AND ROME; THE ETHICS OF JUDAISM AND ISLAM (Section D: Moral Decision-making, Chapter 5)

OPENING QUOTE
- "Let us be moral, let us contemplate existence." (Charles Dickens)

THE GREEKS - INTRODUCTION
- It is said that WESTERN CIVILISATION BEGAN WITH THE GREEKS. Greek thought shapes us in ways we may not realise.
- Example: the OLYMPIC GAMES began in Greece, embodying the pursuit of sporting excellence - the driving force of the modern Olympic movement.
- Irony: the Olympic ideal struggles with ethics - the abuse of PERFORMANCE-ENHANCING DRUGS. The real Olympic spirit may be best shown in the SPECIAL OLYMPICS, hosted in Ireland in summer 2003.
- Greek writers on ethics: Aristotle, Plato, Socrates, the Stoics, the Cynics, the Sceptics, the Epicureans and the Sophists. Their ways of thinking shape how we think now.

SOCRATES AND PLATO
- Early Greek philosophers were concerned with the existence of truth in a changing world.
- SOCRATES (470-399 BCE) and his pupil PLATO (428-347 BCE) were more concerned with HOW LIFE SHOULD BE LIVED - with ethics.
- They believed KNOWLEDGE IS TRUTH: once you knew the truth, you would do the right action.
- NO ONE DOES WRONG WILLINGLY: we may think a wrong action is right out of IGNORANCE, or be clouded by PASSION. VICE (wrongdoing) is the result of IGNORANCE.
- Socrates distinguished OPINION (what I think is right) from TRUTH (what I know is correct). Opinion changes; truth is fixed. (Ann Walsh, "Believe to Live")
- Assignment: Plato's ALLEGORY OF THE CAVE - about truth and opinion.

ARISTOTLE (384-322 BCE)
- One of the most influential Greek ethical philosophers; especially important to MEDIEVAL CATHOLIC MORAL THEOLOGY and to THOMAS AQUINAS. His ideas still matter today.
- Entered PLATO'S ACADEMY aged SEVENTEEN and stayed until Plato's death in 347 BCE.
- Was TUTOR to the young ALEXANDER THE GREAT, then founded his own school, the LYCEUM, in Athens. We have summaries of his lectures.
- Ethics studies the good for human beings and is part of POLITICAL or SOCIAL SCIENCE.
- Two most important works: NICOMACHEAN ETHICS (Nicomachus was his son) and POLITICS.
Aristotle's teachings
- ON NATURE: nature produces nothing without a PURPOSE. The purpose of every object is to be itself in the fullest sense - to REALISE ITS POTENTIAL.
- ON THE SOUL: every living thing has PSYCHE (soul). The soul is FORM, the body MATTER. Our souls give us the potential to reach our true end, which for humans is HAPPINESS.
- ON ETHICS: VIRTUE (ARETE) is EXCELLENCE in fulfilling one's proper task or purpose. What is special to humans is our capacity to REASON, so we must develop our INTELLECTUAL and MORAL virtues.
- WE BECOME VIRTUOUS BY DOING VIRTUOUS THINGS. We start doing them out of COMPULSION; through EDUCATION and HABIT we grow to do them because we believe them right and good.
- Great emphasis on TRAINING by PARENTS, TEACHERS and the STATE.
- Living the good life means acting in accordance with moral virtue.
- ON POLITICS: he did NOT value DEMOCRACY because it values private interests over the common interest. The good of the STATE is more important than the good of the individual because it secures the good of the many.
- His chief moral concern: LIVING A VIRTUOUS LIFE.
- (Discussion question: is Aristotle's ethics teleological or deontological?)

THE CYNICS
- A Cynic had NO DESIRE OTHER THAN THE DESIRE FOR GOODNESS - different from how we use the word today!
- VIRTUE IS ALL THAT MATTERS. It is not just theory but ACTION. If determined, a person can achieve virtue. Everything is secondary to pursuing virtue.
- Even LOVE should not get in the way, because it can make one a SLAVE TO ONE'S PASSIONS.
- The cynic ANTISTHENES said of Aphrodite, Greek god of love: "If I could lay my hands on Aphrodite, I would shoot her!"

THE EPICUREANS
- The goal of life is HAPPINESS, in particular PLEASURE. Pleasure is the ONLY GOOD that exists.
- But they did NOT seek physical pleasure whenever they could. Pure pleasure was the CALM SERENITY present when the SOUL IS AT PEACE.
- So they lived SIMPLE and AUSTERE lives. Falling in love would disturb your peace, so avoid it. Entering POLITICS did not lead to a peaceful life, so shun it. "Serenity and peace at all costs!"

THE ROMANS - THE STOICS
- The greatest influence on Roman ethics was the STOICS, who began in Greece.
- The Stoic school was set up in ATHENS about 300 BCE by ZENO OF CITIUM.
- PANAETIUS introduced Stoicism to ROME.
- Roman Stoics: CATO THE YOUNGER; during the Empire, three whose writings survive - SENECA, EPICTETUS and the emperor MARCUS AURELIUS. The orator MARCUS TULLIUS CICERO (106-43 BCE) was also a Stoic.
- They made ETHICS the main field of knowledge, but developed LOGIC and NATURAL SCIENCE to support it.
- They believed the divine, God, was EVERYWHERE, in everyone, and everything is arranged and settled by God. So we must live according to the WILL OF GOD or the WILL OF NATURE - accepting God's will as shown in nature.
- Epictetus: "He does not will it, I do not wish it."
- GOODNESS is the ACCEPTANCE OF THE WILL OF GOD, expressed in the events of the world. Living according to nature or reason = living in conformity with the DIVINE ORDER of the universe.
- The Stoics influenced the beginning of NATURAL LAW theory, which affected ROMAN LAW.
- FOUR CARDINAL VIRTUES (influenced by Plato): WISDOM, COURAGE, JUSTICE and TEMPERANCE.
- They did NOT value the EMOTIONS; people should be cleansed of emotion to serve God's will better.
- ONE UNIVERSAL SPIRIT in all people, so all should live in MUTUAL LOVE and help each other; RANK and WEALTH are of no importance.
- So, BEFORE CHRISTIANITY, the Stoics recognised our COMMON HUMANITY and the NATURAL EQUALITY of all people.
- Discussion: "The key to happiness is to learn to want what we have!"

STOIC TEACHING ON WAR - CICERO
- CICERO's work DE OFFICIIS has a clear teaching on JUSTIFYING WAR, which later influenced AUGUSTINE in the early Church.
- The only cause for war: that we might LIVE UNHARMED IN PEACE.
- After victory, MERCY should be shown to the defeated.
- No war unless there has been an OFFICIAL DEMAND FOR SATISFACTION or a FORMAL DECLARATION following an appropriate WARNING.
- War could be fought to PRESERVE THE SAFETY OF A CITY, PROTECT THE INNOCENT, AVENGE WRONGS and HONOUR PLEDGES TO ALLIES.

JEWISH/HEBREW ETHICS
Scripture
- Judaism is very important and influential; it shaped Jewish lives and hugely influenced religions that grew from its scriptures.
- Morality is an INTRINSIC part of Jewish faith, shaped by the TORAH.
- Unlike the GREEKS, who treated ethics as a separate category and wrote specifically on it, for the biblical authors HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY DERIVES FROM THE REALITY OF GOD.
Adam and Eve - good and evil (Genesis 2:4 to end of chapter 3)
- The serpent: "You will not die; for God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil." (Genesis 3:4-5)
- (The chapter asks: what fruit is actually mentioned? Read the text!)
- Message: God GIVES LIFE, creates beauty and abundance, and gives COMMANDS. Eating of the tree brings death. People are FREE but TEMPTED by evil (the serpent). When they sin they are ASHAMED and CUT OFF from the beauty of the garden.
- So MORALITY IS PART OF A PERSON'S RELATIONSHIP WITH GOD (as in the Covenant and the Decalogue).
- God seeks REPENTANCE and desires JUSTICE - from all people.
- No one conquers the will to do evil, even MOSES (Exodus 2:11).
- God cares how people act: God "roars, cries, regrets, rages and threatens" in response to sin (Amos 1). God cares about the GENTILES (non-Jews) too.
God of Justice
- Justice is a powerful theme. Personal and social INJUSTICES are condemned as SINFUL. The psalms cry for justice (Psalms 9 and 10; Amos 1:6; Micah).
- God is concerned for the POWERLESS: the WIDOW, the ORPHAN, the STRANGER. The community must care for the poor.
- Psalm 91 (the hymn "On Eagle's Wings") expresses God's care.
The Torah
- Revered by Jews; contains THE LAW. The FIRST FIVE BOOKS of the Bible: GENESIS, EXODUS, LEVITICUS, NUMBERS and DEUTERONOMY.
- Tells of God's actions for the people and how the people must respond.
- Torah laws to examine: Leviticus 11, 13, 19; Deuteronomy 8, 16, 18, 22.

CHARACTERISTICS OF JUDAIC ETHICS
- FREEDOM: valued since the EXODUS; highlighted by continual PERSECUTION, right up to the GHETTOS of European cities in the twentieth century. Also PERSONAL freedom - the right to shape one's own destiny.
- JUSTICE: a passion for justice and righteousness. Belief in the KINSHIP OF ALL PEOPLES should show in CHARITY, COMPASSION and KINDNESS. Inhumanity is an affront to a God of justice. The TALMUD: "Why does this workman ascend the highest scaffolding and risk his life, if you do not pay him his wages as soon as they are due?"
- REVERENCE FOR LIFE: reverence for all life and holiness are distinctive values. Life is SACRED.
- To save a life, EVERY law in the Torah can be broken EXCEPT THREE: IDOLATRY, MURDER and SEXUAL IMMORALITY.
- The FOETUS: Judaism generally believes it does not become a person until BIRTH, so if the MOTHER'S LIFE is directly threatened, ABORTION IS ALLOWED.
- EUTHANASIA: the dying patient's end should NOT BE HASTENED. The Talmud: he who shoots a man as he falls off a cliff is guilty of MURDER, even though the man would die anyway.

JUDAISM TODAY
- About FOURTEEN MILLION Jews worldwide: SIX MILLION in the USA and 4.7 MILLION in ISRAEL. A small Jewish community in Ireland.
- Earliest record of Jews in Ireland: the ANNALS OF INISFALLEN (by monks on the Lakes of Killarney) record that in 1079 FIVE JEWS came over the sea with gifts for the grandson of BRIAN BORU - and were sent back!
- Now a SYNAGOGUE and community in DUBLIN with a CHIEF RABBI, and a synagogue in CORK.
- The HOLOCAUST (Nazi extermination of Jews) and ZIONISM (the movement to create and maintain a Jewish state) have profoundly shaped how Jews see themselves today.
Jewish practice
- Ritual is important. The SHEMA (Deuteronomy 6:4-9) is read every MORNING and EVENING by devout Jews.
- On entering and leaving home Jews touch the MEZUZAH, a small case containing the words of the Shema.

ISLAMIC ETHICS
- Islam is one of the great MONOTHEISTIC religions, sharing much tradition and belief with Judaism and Christianity.
Sources
- For the Muslim, ALL OF LIFE IS UNDER THE AUTHORITY OF GOD (ALLAH); one must live according to God's will. An action is COMMANDED or FORBIDDEN by God.
- The QUR'AN - the revealed word of God, communicated in the SEVENTH CENTURY CE through the prophet MUHAMMAD - is the ULTIMATE CRITERION for good and evil.
- MUHAMMAD is the HIGHEST EXAMPLE OF HUMAN VIRTUE.
- Islamic ethics is based mainly on the Qur'an and the traditions of Muhammad, the HADITH. A famous hadith: "ACTIONS ARE JUDGED BY THE INTENTION."
- The SUNNA: a major text SECOND ONLY TO THE QUR'AN, based on the SAYINGS, ACTIONS and APPROVALS of Muhammad. Muslims follow his example (Sunna) in close detail.

VIRTUES, VICES, HALAL AND HARAM
- Virtues, if allowed to flourish, lead to goodness; vices, left unchecked, lead to evil.
- VIRTUES: justice, sincerity, wisdom, mercy and compassion, courage, love, hope and patience.
- VICES: pride, slander, strong anger, gluttony, excess in sexual relations, cursing, excessive speech, envy and love of wealth.
- The Qur'an is not just a list of good and evil but a SCHEME OF LIFE to make sure good triumphs.
- HALAL: what is lawful (e.g. can be eaten). HARAM: what is not lawful. The Qur'an defines halal, which is very close to the Jewish idea of KOSHER. ALCOHOL is HARAM.

THE FIVE PILLARS - ZAKAT
- The central beliefs of Islam are the FIVE PILLARS OF FAITH. Ethically the most interesting is ZAKAT, the GIVING OF ALMS.
- "Zakat" means PURIFICATION and GROWTH. Possessions are purified by setting aside a PERCENTAGE for those in need.
- ZAKAT OF SELF: given before the end of RAMADAN.
- ZAKAT OF WEALTH: given at YEAR'S END by those with surplus wealth.
- ALL THINGS BELONG TO ALLAH; those with wealth keep it IN TRUST.

ISLAMIC STATES
- Some states - SAUDI ARABIA, PAKISTAN and IRAN - seek to base state law SOLELY on Qur'anic legislation, seeing it as a religious duty to form an Islamic state where Muslims are the majority and to spread Muhammad's message. Other branches are more open. This poses problems, even in Britain with its significant Muslim minority.
- Such countries argue they respect the UN Charter and Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and that the Qur'an already respects non-Muslims' rights. It gives a special place to the "PEOPLE OF THE BOOK" (Jews and Christians): "our God and your God is One and it is to Him we bow." (Qur'an 29:46)
- The UNIVERSAL DECLARATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS IN ISLAM (1981) addresses modern questions using the Qur'an and hadith.

SHARIA LAW
- SHARIA means "CLEAR PATH": religious law governing belief, worship, and social and individual morality.
- FOUR SOURCES: the QUR'AN; the SUNNA; the IJMA (consensus of the community and its scholars); the QIYAS (deductions from the first three).
- Two types of duty: INDIVIDUAL and COLLECTIVE.
- FIVE CATEGORIES of actions: OBLIGATORY; RECOMMENDED but not obligatory; NEUTRAL or permitted; DISAPPROVED; FORBIDDEN (HARAM).
State law and the Sharia
- Not a uniform, codified system; interpreted very differently from INDONESIA to IRAN.
- Islam has slowly adapted to Western law codes, enforced in SECULAR COURTS; only FAMILY LAW remains for Sharia courts. Most Islamic countries EXCEPT SAUDI ARABIA now have secular laws influenced by Islam.
- But a growing desire to return to strict Sharia: AFGHANISTAN under the TALIBAN and NIGERIA imposed it on all citizens.
- 2002: a woman in a northern province of NIGERIA was sentenced to DEATH BY STONING for ADULTERY under Sharia. A higher court REVERSED it because she had not been properly represented and the adultery was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
- Extreme Islamic FUNDAMENTALISM has expressed itself in violence: killings in BALI, TURKEY and the PHILIPPINES and the 11 SEPTEMBER 2001 attacks. The VAST MAJORITY of Muslims REJECT this.
- JIHAD (holy war) is often used as an excuse, but jihad also means a STRUGGLE AGAINST EVIL INCLINATIONS OF THE SOUL (Qur'an 12:53).

SHIRIN EBADI
- Awarded the NOBEL PEACE PRIZE in 2003 for efforts for DEMOCRACY and HUMAN RIGHTS, especially the rights of WOMEN and CHILDREN.
- A LAWYER, JUDGE, LECTURER, WRITER and ACTIVIST in IRAN; ignored threats to her own safety.
- Supports NON-VIOLENCE; believes supreme political power must rest on DEMOCRATIC ELECTIONS; favours ENLIGHTENMENT and DIALOGUE.
- A conscious Muslim who sees NO CONFLICT BETWEEN ISLAM AND FUNDAMENTAL HUMAN RIGHTS. Dialogue between cultures should start from SHARED VALUES.
- The FIRST citizen of Iran to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Her choice highlights developments within Islam.

SUMMARY
- The chief moral concern of the great Greek philosophers was the search for VIRTUE and HAPPINESS.
- Plato and Socrates: truth is found in knowledge; know the truth and you will do right.
- Aristotle: virtue is found by doing virtuous things.
- The Stoics of Rome accepted the will of God shown in nature.
- Jewish and Islamic ethics are founded on their scriptures and traditions.

KEY TERMS
- Ethics: the study of the good for human beings (for Aristotle, part of political/social science).
- Virtue (arete): excellence in fulfilling one's proper task or purpose.
- Cynic: a person with no desire other than the desire for goodness/virtue.
- Stoics: school founded by Zeno about 300 BCE; goodness is accepting God's will shown in nature.
- Torah: the first five books of the Bible, containing the Law.
- Qur'an: the revealed word of God through Muhammad; the ultimate criterion of good and evil in Islam.
- Hadith: the traditions of the prophet Muhammad.
- Sunna: the sayings, actions and approvals of Muhammad; second only to the Qur'an.
- Halal: what is lawful in Islam.
- Haram: what is unlawful/forbidden in Islam.
- Zakat: almsgiving; means purification and growth; one of the Five Pillars.
- Sharia: "clear path"; Islamic religious law with four sources.

rows.prompt: Explain what Socrates and Plato believed about knowledge and wrongdoing.
rows.model_answer: They believed knowledge is truth: once you know the truth, you will do the right action. No one does wrong willingly; we do wrong out of ignorance or because we are clouded by passion. So vice is the result of ignorance.

rows.prompt: How does a person live a good life according to Aristotle?
rows.model_answer: By developing intellectual and moral virtue (arete), which is excellence in fulfilling one's purpose. We become virtuous by doing virtuous things - first out of compulsion, then through education and habit, until we do them because we believe them right. Parents, teachers and the State play a big part in this training.

rows.prompt: Compare what the Cynics and the Epicureans valued most.
rows.model_answer: The Cynics valued virtue above everything, even love, which could make one a slave to passion. The Epicureans valued pleasure, but understood it as the calm serenity of a soul at peace, so they lived simple lives and avoided love and politics.

rows.prompt: What attitude did the Stoics have to ethics?
rows.model_answer: They made ethics the main field of knowledge. They believed God was everywhere and arranged everything, so goodness is accepting God's will as shown in nature. They held four cardinal virtues - wisdom, courage, justice and temperance - and believed in one universal spirit, so all people are equal.

rows.prompt: What are the main characteristics of Jewish ethical thought?
rows.model_answer: Freedom, valued since the Exodus and through centuries of persecution. Justice, a passion for righteousness shown in charity, compassion and kindness. Reverence for life, which is sacred: every Torah law except three can be broken to save a life.

rows.prompt: What role does the Sunna play in Islamic ethics?
rows.model_answer: The Sunna is a major text second only to the Qur'an. It is based on the sayings, actions and approvals of the prophet Muhammad, who is the highest example of human virtue. Muslims follow his example in close detail.

rows.prompt: Explain the terms halal and haram, with an example.
rows.model_answer: Halal means what is lawful, such as food Muslims may eat; it is close to the Jewish idea of kosher. Haram means what is not lawful or forbidden. For example, alcohol is haram.

rows.prompt: Outline the ethical teaching of Aristotle and assess whether it is teleological. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Aristotle (384-322 BCE) studied at Plato's Academy, tutored Alexander the Great and founded the Lyceum in Athens. His key works are Nicomachean Ethics and Politics. He was hugely important to medieval Catholic moral theology and to Thomas Aquinas. For Aristotle, ethics studies the good for human beings and is part of political science. Nature produces nothing without a purpose: the purpose of everything is to realise its potential. Every living thing has a psyche, or soul; the soul is form and the body matter, and our souls give us the potential to reach our true end, which is happiness. Virtue (arete) is excellence in fulfilling one's purpose. Since what is special to humans is reason, we must develop intellectual and moral virtues. We become virtuous by doing virtuous things, at first out of compulsion, then through education and habit, until we do them because we believe they are good. Parents, teachers and the State are important trainers. He valued the good of the State over the individual and distrusted democracy. His chief concern was living a virtuous life. His ethics is teleological, because it judges actions by the end or goal (telos) they achieve: human fulfilment and happiness.

rows.prompt: Describe the main features of Stoic ethics and their influence on later thought. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The Stoic school was founded in Athens about 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium, and Panaetius brought it to Rome, where it became the greatest influence on Roman ethics. Famous Stoics include Cato the Younger, Seneca, Epictetus, the emperor Marcus Aurelius and Cicero. The Stoics made ethics the main field of knowledge, supported by logic and natural science. They believed God was everywhere and arranged everything, so we must live according to the will of God shown in nature. Epictetus said, 'He does not will it, I do not wish it.' Goodness is accepting God's will; living by nature or reason means conforming to the divine order. Their four cardinal virtues were wisdom, courage, justice and temperance, influenced by Plato. They did not value emotion and thought people should be cleansed of it. Because there is one universal spirit in all, people should live in mutual love; rank and wealth do not matter. So before Christianity they recognised common humanity and equality. Their influence was great: they began Natural Law theory, which shaped Roman law. Cicero's De Officiis taught that war is only for living unharmed in peace, needs a formal declaration after warning, and calls for mercy after victory; this influenced Augustine.

rows.prompt: Outline the sources and main characteristics of Jewish ethics. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Morality is an intrinsic part of Jewish faith, shaped by scripture, the Torah - the first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. It tells of God's actions for the people and how they must respond. Unlike the Greeks, who treated ethics as a separate subject, the biblical authors saw human responsibility as coming from the reality of God. The story of Adam and Eve shows that God gives life and commands; people are free but tempted, and sin leaves them ashamed and cut off. So morality is part of a relationship with God, seen in the Covenant and Decalogue. God desires repentance from everyone, even Moses, and cares about Gentiles too. Justice is a powerful theme: God cares for the widow, the orphan and the stranger, and the psalms cry for justice. The main characteristics are freedom, valued since the Exodus and through persecution; justice, shown in charity and compassion - the Talmud demands workers be paid on time; and reverence for life. Life is sacred: every Torah law except idolatry, murder and sexual immorality may be broken to save a life. Abortion is allowed if the mother's life is threatened, but a dying person's end must not be hastened.

rows.prompt: Discuss the sources of Islamic ethics and the role of Sharia law in Islamic states today. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: For Muslims all of life is under the authority of Allah, and actions are commanded or forbidden by God. The Qur'an, revealed through the prophet Muhammad in the seventh century CE, is the ultimate criterion of good and evil. Muhammad is the highest example of virtue, and his traditions, the hadith, guide Muslims - for example, 'Actions are judged by the intention.' The Sunna, based on his sayings, actions and approvals, is second only to the Qur'an. These sources list virtues such as justice, mercy and patience, and vices such as pride, envy and love of wealth, and define what is halal or haram. Sharia, meaning 'clear path', governs belief, worship and morality. Its four sources are the Qur'an, the Sunna, the ijma (community consensus) and the qiyas (deductions). It sorts actions into obligatory, recommended, neutral, disapproved and forbidden. It is interpreted very differently from Indonesia to Iran. Most Islamic countries, except Saudi Arabia, now have secular laws influenced by Islam, with Sharia courts only for family law. But some, like Afghanistan under the Taliban and Nigeria, imposed strict Sharia; in 2002 a Nigerian woman was sentenced to stoning for adultery, later reversed. Shirin Ebadi shows that Islam and human rights need not conflict.

rows.prompt: Explain the practice of zakat and its ethical significance in Islam. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The central beliefs of Islam are summed up in the Five Pillars of Faith. From an ethical point of view the most interesting is zakat, the giving of alms. The word zakat means purification and growth: a person's possessions are purified by setting aside a percentage for those in need. There are two kinds. The zakat of self is given before the end of the month of Ramadan. The zakat of wealth is given at the end of the year by those who have surplus wealth. Its ethical significance is that all things belong to Allah, so those who have wealth only keep it in trust. Zakat expresses justice and compassion, virtues listed in the Qur'an, and guards against the vice of love of wealth. It shows that the Qur'an is a scheme of life to make sure good triumphs.
